title: Wi-Fi Standards and Bands: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: B, G, N, A C, A X. Wi Fi standards look like alphabet soup. Let's make sense of them.

lines.t: b, g, n, a c, a x

scenes.heading: Highways getting wider
scenes.narration: Think of Wi Fi standards as an upgrading highway system. The data rate is the speed limit. But real speed depends on traffic and road conditions, which is interference. Each new standard widens the road, and adds smarter lanes. Even so, you'll only ever get about half the posted speed in real life.

scenes.heading: The family tree
scenes.narration: Here's the list in order. Eight oh two dot eleven b is old, with eleven megabits, on two point four gigahertz. Then a and g reach fifty-four. N is called Wi Fi four, and reaches six hundred. A C is Wi Fi five, and lives only on five gigahertz. And A X is Wi Fi six, which adds the six gigahertz band.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three slip-ups. A C works only on five gigahertz. Wider channels aren't always better, because you get fewer that don't overlap. On two point four, there are only three clear channels, one, six and eleven. And N goes up to six hundred megabits, not fifty-four.

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva Wi-Fi standards lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Each Wi Fi standard is a wider, smarter road. A C is five gigahertz only, and A X adds six gigahertz. On two point four, stick to channels one, six and eleven. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva Wi-Fi standards lab.
